The Healing of the Paralytic

Icons

Scriptural scenes

The Healing of the Paralytic

Sunday of the Paralytic · The Pool of Bethesda

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

John 5:1–15

King James Version · Scripture previews

The selected historic Greek icon identifies the Sunday of the Paralytic. Its pool setting belongs to John 5’s Bethesda account, rather than the roof-opening scene of Mark 2.

What is depicted

Christ addresses the man before a walled pool, while the healed man is shown with his bed. The file identifies the panel at Saint Paraskevi Church in Langadas and dates it before the twentieth century.

History and tradition

And a certain man was there, which had an infirmity thirty and eight years.

When Jesus saw him lie, and knew that he had been now a long time in that case, he saith unto him, Wilt thou be made whole?

The impotent man answered him, Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me.

Jesus saith unto him, Rise, take up thy bed, and walk.

And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath.

[2] John 5:5–9

Published explanation

Afterward Jesus findeth him in the temple, and said unto him, Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee.

The man departed, and told the Jews that it was Jesus, which had made him whole.

The Gospel’s subsequent meeting in the Temple; no extra symbolic meaning is assigned to the pool architecture or painted colors.

[2] John 5:14–15
